coredata.dc:description: Ground source heat pump (GSHP) systems, while renowned for their efficiency as renewable energy sources, can experience soil heat imbalance issues during prolonged use. Solar-coupled ground source heat pump (SGSHP) systems have been introduced to mitigate these imbalances by incorporating solar energy to enhance the overall system performance. However, SGSHP systems often face economic challenges because of their high initial and operational costs, thus making them less suitable for use in large-scale heating applications. To address these challenges, this study examines how underground pipe spacing impacts the thermal performance and the economic viability of both GSHP and SGSHP systems. Numerical simulations were conducted using fork models with pipe spacings of 4 m, 4.6 m, and 5.2 m. A comprehensive annual simulation was conducted to evaluate thermal characteristics in the subsurface and at ground level. During the secondary heating phase, spatial temperature variations at 49.5 m below surface were systematically examined alongside surface thermal patterns through cloud visualization and scatter plot analysis. The results revealed that increasing the underground pipe spacing reduces soil heat accumulation, improves the thermal balance, and enhances the heat transfer efficiency for both systems. Economically, pipe spacings of up to 4.6 m maintain cost-effectiveness for GSHP systems, but greater spacings lead to diminished economic performance and extended payback periods. This study provides actionable insights for pipe spacing optimization in the design of both GSHP and SGSHP systems and offers a practical pathway toward improved thermal efficiency and economic feasibility.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Ground source heat pump (GSHP) systems, while renowned for their efficiency as renewable energy sources, can experience soil heat imbalance issues during prolonged use. Solar-coupled ground source heat pump (SGSHP) systems have been introduced to mitigate these imbalances by incorporating solar energy to enhance the overall system performance. However, SGSHP systems often face economic challenges because of their high initial and operational costs, thus making them less suitable for use in large-scale heating applications. To address these challenges, this study examines how underground pipe spacing impacts the thermal performance and the economic viability of both GSHP and SGSHP systems. Numerical simulations were conducted using fork models with pipe spacings of 4 m, 4.6 m, and 5.2 m. A comprehensive annual simulation was conducted to evaluate thermal characteristics in the subsurface and at ground level. During the secondary heating phase, spatial temperature variations at 49.5 m below surface were systematically examined alongside surface thermal patterns through cloud visualization and scatter plot analysis. The results revealed that increasing the underground pipe spacing reduces soil heat accumulation, improves the thermal balance, and enhances the heat transfer efficiency for both systems. Economically, pipe spacings of up to 4.6 m maintain cost-effectiveness for GSHP systems, but greater spacings lead to diminished economic performance and extended payback periods. This study provides actionable insights for pipe spacing optimization in the design of both GSHP and SGSHP systems and offers a practical pathway toward improved thermal efficiency and economic feasibility.

ce:section.ce:para: Global consumption of fossil fuels is continuing to rise, leading to increasing carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. Many countries worldwide consume huge amounts of energy, with the construction industry accounting for 20∼40% of the total energy consumed (Kharseh et al., 2015; Al-Khoury and Focaccia, 2016; Hu et al., 2016; Safa et al., 2015). Mitigation of the negative effects of carbon emissions on the environment is thus essential. Reducing fossil fuel consumption and optimizing the energy mix through active renewable energy source usage will help countries to meet this requirement (Ozyurt and Ekinci, 2011). To tackle these energy challenges and support sustainable development, it is important to cut back on fossil fuel use and shift toward cleaner alternative energy sources. Zoelly et al. initially presented the ground source heat pump (GSHP) concept in 1912 (Bose and Parker, 1983). As an environmentally sustainable technology, GSHP systems significantly decrease reliance on fossil fuels while minimizing ecological impact, owing to their reduced carbon footprint and low environmental externalities (Yousefi et al., 2017; Doranehgard et al., 2017; Saffarzadeh and Noorollahi, 2005). These systems play a crucial role in mitigating energy-related emissions and supporting ecological conservation efforts (Wu and Skye, 2018; Saeidi et al., 2018).The stability, efficiency, and cleanliness of GSHP systems make them a compelling choice for government investment (Chong et al., 2013; Morino and Oka, 1994; Yoon et al., 2015) and have driven their accelerated development (Zhu et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2024).

GSHP systems perform best in regions where heating and cooling needs are evenly spread throughout the year. However, in China, numerous buildings are located in regions primarily requiring either heating or cooling. This can cause an imbalance between the heat drawn from and rejected by the soil (Hou et al., 2024). This discrepancy could result in challenges like soil temperature fluctuations causing an imbalance in soil heat. This also reducing the efficiency of the heat pump units (Wu et al., 2014). Dai et al. studied a GSHP system for five years to tackle these issues (Dai et al., 2015), while Yin et al. assessed the performances of multiple systems (Yin et al., 2019). Similarly, Naranjo-Mendoza et al. conducted GSHP monitoring using a test system (İnall and Esen, 2004). These studies consistently found that in regions with imbalanced cooling and heating demands, prolonged GSHP system operation leads to ground thermal imbalances that ultimately reduce system efficiency. To keep the soil's thermal balance and ensure GSHP operate at an optimal coefficient of performance (COP) level, supplemental heat energy must be added to the soil (Allaerts et al., 2015).

To address soil thermal imbalances and ground heat accumulation, several researchers have suggested integrating solar collectors along with GSHP systems. This approach involves storing heat by injecting solar energy into the ground (Naranjo-Mendoza et al., 2019). The concept of seasonal solar energy storage was first introduced in the USA during the 1960s, with full research projects following in the 1970s. By the 1980s, this type of storage system had also attracted the attention of researchers in Northern European countries. Fine et al. conducted an in-depth study on solar-coupled ground source heat pump (SGSHP) systems. The results show that when the cooling and heating load ratio of the building reaches 1.2:1, the applicability of this system is limited (Fine et al., 2018). In addition to the load ratio, economic factors also play critical roles in determining system feasibility. Moreover, the underground pipe spacing has significant effects on both soil temperature regulation and heat exchange efficiency (Bai and Che, 2016). Few studies have simultaneously considered both net economic performance and dynamic investment payback period when evaluating underground pipe spacing and its impact on heat transfer performance and soil thermal accumulation in heat pump systems. In practice, the promotion and application of heat pump systems are governed primarily by two key indicators: economic viability and heat transfer efficiency, which often exhibit inherent trade-offs in system design. However, existing research on GSHP and SGSHP systems has largely focused on either thermal performance evaluation or soil thermal imbalance mitigation in isolation. Limited attention has been given to the coupled effects of borehole spacing optimization, solar-assisted heat injection, and system-level economic–thermal trade-offs under consistent boundary conditions.

This study investigates the thermal performance and economic feasibility of GSHP and SGSHP systems in a large building located in Hebei Province, China (119°53'E, 42°37'N). A unified numerical model is developed to evaluate and compare the heat transfer characteristics of both systems, with a focus on soil heat storage, heat extraction, and system-level performance under consistent boundary conditions. The novelty of this study lies in three aspects: (1) a unified numerical framework is established to enable a consistent comparison between GSHP and SGSHP systems under identical boundary conditions; (2) the effects of borehole spacing on soil thermal accumulation and heat transfer performance are systematically quantified; and (3) a coupled thermo-economic assessment is conducted to evaluate the practical applicability of solar-assisted systems in cold-region buildings.

The investigated system is a SGSHP system installed in the basement of a major university library. The system serves a building area of approximately 49,000 m2, while the boreholes area covers about 27,000 m2. The key parameters of building envelope and occupancy conditions are listed in Table 1. As shown in Fig. 1, the integrated system combines a ground source heat pump (GSHP) unit with solar-thermal collectors. The solar subsystem is designed to supplement the GSHP operation by injecting additional heat into the ground during non-heating seasons, thereby improving long-term thermal balance and heat transfer performance. The SGSHP system consists of two main components: an above-ground system and an underground pipe system. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the above-ground system includes a circulation pump for air conditioning and underfloor heating, a ground source-side circulation pump, and a heat pump unit. The underground pipe system, shown in Fig. 1(b), consists of a borehole heat exchanger network that uses the surrounding soil as a heat source in winter and a heat sink in summer. The borehole field is divided into 16 sections and includes a total of 1200 boreholes with a depth of 100 m. The parameters of the underground pipe system are summarized in Table 2.

Based on the practical project described in 2, the numerical model of the GSHP system and the SGSHP system was built. The model was created to assess and contrast the heat transfer efficiencies of both systems, concentrating on their heat storage and extraction processes under different conditions. The SGSHP system integrates solar energy collection to enable seasonal heat storage in the ground. During warm seasons (i.e., spring, summer, and autumn), solar-heated water circulates through the underground pipes to charge the soil thermal reservoir. In winter, cooler fluid is circulated to extract the stored heat for building heating. The key parameters of the solar-thermal subsystem are summarized in Table 3. In contrast, the GSHP system operation is based purely on the use of geothermal energy, with heat being transferred to the soil in summer and extracted in winter, without the need for additional external energy inputs.

To investigate the impacts of the GSHP and SGSHP systems on soil heat accumulation, the U-shaped underground pipe and the surrounding soil were simulated. Yanping et al. (2016) demonstrated that the heat fluxes of the underground pipes differ at different locations within the underground pipe cluster, and the soil's heat accumulation behavior is correspondingly affected by these spatially varying heat fluxes. Therefore, the thermal effects of the underground pipes on the surrounding soil differ depending on their location within the pipe cluster.

Due to the limitations of computational resources, constructing a full-scale numerical model comprising 1200 underground pipes is impractical. The present study therefore adopts a simplified single U-shaped pipe model, which is well-supported by established theory and prior literature. Specifically, Katsura et al. (2008) demonstrated, based on linear heat source theory, that the soil temperature response of a multiple-pipe group can be obtained by the superposition of the thermal responses of individual pipes, confirming that the fundamental heat transfer mechanism of a single pipe is consistent with that of a pipe cluster. Building on this principle, Shang et al. (2011) successfully predicted the soil temperature evolution during both the operation and recovery periods of a GSHP system using a three-dimensional single-well, single-U-tube model, and showed that the key controlling factors-particularly soil thermophysical properties—exert the same influence regardless of whether a single or multiple pipes are considered. Furthermore, as explicitly stated in recent work on middle-shallow borehole ground heat exchangers, the heat transfer of multiple boreholes is the superposition of all single-borehole cases (Bernier et al., 2008). The primary difference between a single-pipe model and a multi-pipe group therefore lies in the magnitude of thermal interaction, while the underlying heat transfer mechanism remains consistent under linear superposition conditions This is consistent with the long-established use of simplified single-borehole models for parametric studies of pipe spacing and operational control strategies in the ground source heat pump literature (He and Lam, 2016).

Accordingly, the underground pipe model was simplified to a single U-shaped pipe configuration to compare the effects of underground pipe spacing and the control of heat extraction and storage processes on the soil temperature under long-term operation. The model includes the fluid inside the pipe, a single U-shaped pipe, the backfill, and the surrounding soil, which are arranged sequentially from the inside in the outward direction, as shown in Fig. 2. The basic physical property parameters of the soil and backfill materials that were used in the model are listed in Table 4.
Underground pipe heat exchange occurs in two ways: convective heat transfer from the internal fluid, and thermal conductivity transferring heat from the fluid to the soil through the pipe wall.

Based on the above boundary condition settings and the long-term operational characteristics of ground heat transfer systems, the numerical model is developed under several simplifying assumptions to ensure computational efficiency while preserving the essential physical behavior of the system. First, the surrounding soil is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic at the representative scale of heat diffusion, such that heat transfer is dominated by conduction. Groundwater seepage and advective heat transport are neglected, as the groundwater velocity at the study site is sufficiently low, leading to a negligible contribution of convective heat transfer. Second, the thermophysical properties of the soil, including density, specific heat capacity, and thermal conductivity, are assumed to remain constant during operation. This assumption is considered reasonable given the relatively limited temperature variation in the system, and it avoids introducing additional nonlinear coupling effects. Finally, the heat transfer process is simplified by neglecting axial heat conduction along the borehole depth and assuming axisymmetric temperature distribution around the borehole center. This reduction is applicable for long boreholes under conditions where radial heat transfer dominates, thereby allowing the system to be approximated as a one-dimensional radial conduction problem in the horizontal plane. Under these assumptions, the heat transfer equation for the soil located outside the borehole is given by Eq. (3):

Similar to the surrounding soil domain, the heat transfer model within the borehole is also established under several simplifying assumptions to balance computational efficiency and physical representativeness. The backfill material is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic, with constant thermophysical properties (density, specific heat capacity, and thermal conductivity) over the considered operating temperature range. Groundwater seepage is neglected, as its influence on heat transfer within the borehole region is insignificant under the low-permeability conditions of the surrounding formation. In addition, axial heat conduction within the borehole is neglected, and an axisymmetric temperature field is assumed as an equivalent representation of the borehole thermal behavior. Under this assumption, the borehole domain is simplified to a one-dimensional radial conduction problem in the backfill region. The thermal interaction between the heat carrier fluid and the surrounding backfill is represented by an equivalent heat exchange term, which accounts for the combined effects of fluid convection, pipe wall conduction, and thermal resistance within the borehole system. This coupling term is typically determined based on the temperature difference between the fluid and the borehole wall together with the overall borehole thermal resistance. First, a geometric model of the underground pipe is established, in which the soil is set to have a cylindrical shape and the U-shaped underground pipe is set into the soil; the model is then meshed. The quality of the model meshing directly influences calculation accuracy, and the grid should be segmented according to the heat transfer properties of the underground pipe. The bend section of the underground pipe experiences significant temperature fluctuations, and the rest of the grid in this section needs to be encrypted. The U-shaped underground pipe is divided into four sections that were gridded using a Tet/Hybrid type grid with a spacing of 0.01. The soil temperature changes are comparatively modest and a sparse Tet/Hybrid type grid with spacing of 0.5 was thus used for soil gridding.

The underground pipe was buried at a depth of 100 m, and the underground pipe spacings were set at 4 m, 4.6 m, and 5.2 m, as shown in Fig. 3. In this study, a fork mode was used and the distance between the underground pipes was measured in the vertical direction. The numerical simulation method combines a pressure-based separation solver and a transient process with the addition of the gravitational acceleration of z = −9.8 m/s2. The time step was established at one hour.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Initial conditions, boundary conditions, and parameters
ce:section.ce:para: To ensure the accuracy of the simulation, the following simplifying assumptions were adopted in the model: (1) the soil is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic; (2) groundwater seepage is neglected; (3) the circulating fluid is assumed to be incompressible with constant thermophysical properties. These assumptions are consistent with those adopted in comparable GSHP numerical modeling studies and are considered appropriate given the comparative nature of this study.

The inlets to the underground pipe are set as Inlet-1 and Inlet-2, and the type in this case is Velocity-inlet, which sets the inlet flow rate and the inlet temperature based on the heat exchange process. The outlets from the underground pipe are set as Outlet-1 and Outlet-2, and the type in this case is Outflow. The top of the soil is set as Top with type Wall, which represents an adiabatic boundary layer with a convective heat transfer coefficient heat flux of zero. The soil floor is set as Wall-bottom with type Wall, which again represents an adiabatic boundary layer with a convective heat transfer coefficient heat flux of zero. The lateral boundaries of the soil domain are assigned a constant temperature of 288.87 K (Wall-sides), representing the measured undisturbed far-field ground temperature at the study site prior to system operation. The side and elbow faces of the underground pipe are set as U-side and U-elbow, respectively, which are type Coupled and are connected to the soil. These boundary conditions represent a simplified large-scale soil domain assumption in which lateral heat exchange is negligible and heat transfer is dominated by vertical conduction.

The meteorological data used in this study are based on records from the China Meteorological Administration (CMA) and processed into a representative typical meteorological year (TMY) (GB 50176-2016, 2016). The data are derived according to the latitude and longitude of the studied region. The region is located in northern China and experiences a typical temperate continental climate with four distinct seasons: spring from March to May (approximately 3 months), summer from June to August (approximately 3 months), autumn from September to November (approximately 3 months), and winter from December to February (approximately 3 months). In summer (June to August), the average high temperature is between 30°C and 32°C, with average low temperatures ranging from 20°C to 23°C. In winter (December to February), the average high temperature varies between 7°C and 10°C, with an average low is around −5°C. The exact start and end dates of each season may vary slightly depending on the year and climate fluctuations. However, for northern Chinese cities, the weather in winter and summer is extreme. To ensure indoor comfort, heating and cooling are often started earlier. The winter heating period lasts from mid-November to the end of March, totaling 135 days. Summer is similar, the common cooling duration is 122 days.

The GSHP and SGSHP systems use different heat extraction and heat release scenarios that vary depending on the season; therefore, a user-defined function (UDF) is used to control the heat extraction and release processes. The GSHP extracts heat during the winter and releases heat during the summer without loading the UDF. The cross-seasonal heat storage approach of the SGSHP system involves extracting heat during the winter and then releasing heat in a liquid at 353 K during the spring, summer, and fall, and the UDF program is used to control the 12 h of sunshine used daily to heat the liquid. The system simulation process parameters are listed in Table 5.

To validate the numerical model, thermal response test data from a GSHP system installed in a library in Hebei Province, China were used. The test borehole parameters are listed in Table 6. The borehole requires an effective stabilization test duration of 12 h, and the system consists of a single U-shaped underground pipe with an initial average soil temperature of 288.87 K. During the thermal response test, the inlet temperature was updated every 30 min as part of the standard test protocol. The initial 30-minute period was selected for model validation because it provides a clearly defined and stable boundary condition with a constant inlet temperature of 307.18 K, thereby avoiding the additional uncertainty introduced by the changing inlet conditions in subsequent intervals. Within this period, 50 time steps of 36 s each were simulated, fully capturing the transient thermal response of the system over the 30-minute duration.

The measured outlet temperature after 30 min of system operation was 302.61 K, corresponding to a measured temperature rise of 13.74 K relative to the initial soil temperature of 288.87 K. Under the same boundary conditions, the simulated outlet temperature increased from 288.87 K to 300.64 K, yielding a simulated temperature rise of 11.77 K. The comparison between the simulated and measured outlet temperature profiles over the 30-minute validation period is presented in Fig. 4, which shows good overall agreement between the two datasets. The absolute difference between the simulated and measured temperature rises was 1.97 K, corresponding to a relative error of 14.3%.

This discrepancy is primarily attributed to the simplifying assumptions adopted during model construction. In particular, the influence of groundwater seepage was neglected in the model, whereas in reality groundwater flow enhances heat transfer and results in a higher outlet temperature. Other influencing factors, such as soil heterogeneity and pipe wall thermal resistance, were similarly simplified. Since the primary objective of this study is to comparatively assess the effect of underground pipe spacing and operational control strategies on soil heat exchange characteristics, rather than to predict absolute temperature values, a relative error of 14.3% is considered acceptable. The model is therefore deemed suitable for the intended comparative analysis of different underground pipe spacing configurations.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of underground pipe spacing on the soil surface temperature distribution
ce:section.ce:para: Winter heat extraction and summer heat storage procedures were conducted during the first year of GSHP system operation. The soil’s heat accumulation is reflected directly in the soil’s surface temperature, as shown in Fig. 5. When the underground pipe spacing increases, the high-temperature area on the soil surface also increases significantly, and the high-temperature points are more densely concentrated. This raises the soil temperature until it nearly matches its original state, thereby reducing the thermal imbalance in the soil. This reduction can enhance the system’s heat exchange capacity and is favorable for the heat exchange process used in GSHP systems.

After the second year of cross-seasonal heat storage, the soil surface temperature characteristics of the SGSHP system showed significant changes, as illustrated in Fig. 6. During the first year of thermal storage after heat extraction, the thermal storage fluid temperature reached 353 K and the soil temperature for the SGSHP increased significantly. The high-temperature points provide a visual representation of the soil’s heat accumulation, as illustrated in Fig. 6. As the spacing between the underground pipes increases, the density of high-temperature points also rises. Rising soil temperatures enhance the heat exchange process of the SGSHP system.

The soil surface temperature distributions of the GSHP system and the SGSHP system are compared in Fig. 7. These distributions show that the soil surface temperatures of the two systems differ significantly and that the soil surface temperature of the SGSHP system is significantly higher than that of the GSHP system. After heat storage in the SGSHP system, there will be more dense high-temperature points at the center of the soil surface, and the average temperature of the soil will increase. However, when the underground pipe spacing increases, the difference in the soil surface temperature distribution decreases, and the temperature distribution overlap area between the two systems increases. The gap between the GSHP system and the SGSHP system related to the soil thermal imbalance can be reduced by simply increasing the underground pipe spacing.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of underground pipe spacing on soil (−49.5 m depth) temperature distribution
ce:section.ce:para: Next, the heat extraction and storage processes of the GSHP system and those of an SGSHP system with cross-seasonal heat storage were simulated. The temperature distribution cloud maps after heat extraction during the second year were compared and analyzed to determine the temperature changes that occurred in the horizontal direction in the soil. The underground pipe of the GSHP system is used in the first year to extract heat during the winter and then store heat during the summer. Fig. 8 shows the temperature cloud maps after heat extraction during the second year’s winter. These maps show that, after heat storage, the soil temperature does not increase significantly, and the center temperature of the soil after heat extraction during the second year is lower than the surrounding soil temperature in this case. Because the change in the soil temperature after heat storage is small, the soil’s center temperature is low, and an analysis of the soil temperature cloud maps in the lower-temperature green area for comparison shows that when the underground pipe spacing increases, the radius of influence of this soil cold effect decreases. The radius of influence of the cold effect at the center of the soil is 4 m when the underground pipe spacing is 4 m. The radius of influence of the cold effect at the center of the soil is 2.802 m when the underground pipe spacing is 4.6 m. Finally, when the underground pipe spacing is 5.2 m, the minimum radius of influence of the thermal effect at the center of the soil is 1.782 m. The GSHP system arranged in the fork mode is affected more obviously by the spacing of the underground pipes and as the underground pipe spacing increases, the effect of the cold response on the soil decreases.

Fig. 9 shows the soil temperature distribution cloud maps for the different underground pipe spacings in the SGSHP. The soil cross-section at a depth of 49.5 m below the ground surface was selected as the research object in this case. The cross-seasonal thermal storage pattern of the SGSHP underground pipe in the first year involves heat extraction during winter, followed by heat storage during spring, summer, and fall. The results show that the soil temperature increases after heat storage, and that the center temperature of the soil after heat extraction from the elevated temperature area remains higher than that of the surrounding soil. These soil temperatures can be compared using the size of the soil's high-temperature zone (indicated by the yellow color). This zone shows that the radius of influence of the thermal effect on the soil increases as the spacing between the underground pipes increases. When the underground pipe spacing is 4 m, the minimum spacing for the thermal effect in the middle of the soil is 2.13 m. When the underground pipe spacing is 4.6 m, the minimum spacing for the thermal effect in the middle of the soil is 2.60 m. When the underground pipe spacing is 5.2 m, the minimum spacing for the thermal effect in the middle of the soil is 2.8 m. In the fork mode, the cross-seasonal thermal storage of the SGSHP system is affected more obviously by the underground pipe spacing. Increasing the spacing between the underground pipes of the SGSHP system with inter-seasonal heat storage increases the effect on the soil’s thermal response.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Economic analysis of GSHP system and comparative discussion of SGSHP performance
ce:section.ce:para: In this section, we refer to the findings of Jingyang et al. (2021), whose research was also based on the same engineering project that we have analyzed in this study. To be consistent with their approach, we employed the dynamic evaluation method to gauge the initial investment, yearly operating costs, and estimated revenue of the GSHP system.

Considering the time value and capital flow, the GSHP system is viewed as a long-term investment. To evaluate the project's financial feasibility, we employed a dynamic assessment approach based on net present value (NPV)

The NPV indicates the economic feasibility of the project. The project's investment economic benefits were evaluated by measuring the NPV magnitude.

If the NPV > 0, the scheme is feasible; if not, the scheme will then be rejected. When two investment modes are compared, the scheme with the larger NPV is preferred. The dynamic investment payback period represents the period over which the project’s income can repay the initial investment. A GSHP typically operates for 35 years. Project discount rates usually cap at 15%, with the median rate being around 8% and a fluctuation rate of 1%. The initial investment greatly impacts the NPV; higher upfront costs result in an extended dynamic payback period and unfavorable economic assessment. When the NPV is calculated for the GSHP system for the different underground pipe spacing scenarios, the parameter values should be consistent. Changes in the underground pipe spacing will not affect the cost of purchasing the GSHP system equipment, government subsidies, and other similar factors, but different spacings for the underground pipes can affect the initial investment directly.

In China, the fees for the right to use land are very high, and land is a precious resource. In addition, structures may not be constructed above the underground pipe to enable maintenance and avoid possible collisions. These factors mean that the cost of land use is affected significantly by changes in the spacing of the underground pipes. The costs in this case indicate that the GSHP system was initially planned 20 years ago when the land prices were lower. The land is low-priced land that was specially provided for school construction. Therefore, it is more appropriate to use the required amount of land at the beginning of the investment period. The cost of the land is 120 CNY per square meter. This amount is for land designated exclusively for school development that must be located away from the city center to provide such a low land price. Calculations show that the land areas required were 38,400 m2, 44,592 m2, and 51,648 m2 when the spacings of the underground pipes were 4 m, 4.6 m, and 5.2 m, respectively. The initial investments in the land for these different underground pipe spacings would then be 4608,000 CNY, 5351,040 CNY, and 6197,760 CNY, respectively.

Fig. 10 illustrates that with an underground pipe spacing is 4 m, the NPV stands at 4.14 million CNY, and the investment payback period is projected to be 22 years. However, if the pipe spacing increases to 4.6 m, the NPV drops to 3.26 million CNY and extends the payback period to a lengthy 30 years. When the underground pipe spacing is 5.2 m, the NPV stands at 2.38 million CNY with a payback period exceeding 35 years. Increasing the underground pipe spacing thus extends the dynamic payback period and decreases the economic efficiency of the proposed system.

Building on the previous research (Jingyang et al., 2021), this study provides a fresh perspective by analyzing the way in which varying the underground pipe spacing affects the NPV of a GSHP system, and thus offers valuable insights for optimization of both the economic and thermal performances of the system. Combined with the thermal analysis results presented above, Table 7 provides a comprehensive comparison of the thermal and economic performance of GSHP and SGSHP systems. In this study, the thermal influence radius is used as a unified indicator to characterize the spatial extent of soil temperature disturbance. Although the same metric is adopted for both systems, it reflects different thermal driving mechanisms: cooling-dominated heat extraction in GSHP systems and heat injection-driven diffusion in SGSHP systems. Therefore, variations in the thermal influence radius should be interpreted in the context of system-specific thermal objectives rather than as identical physical processes. Specifically, for GSHP systems, a reduction in the thermal influence radius indicates weakened thermal interference between boreholes and improved mitigation of long-term soil thermal imbalance. In contrast, for SGSHP systems, an increase in the thermal influence radius reflects more effective spatial diffusion of injected solar heat, enhancing subsurface heat storage utilization. These opposite trends are consistent with the distinct operational objectives of the two systems.

When the thermal performance is evaluated together with the dynamic payback period, a clear trade-off relationship can be identified. SGSHP systems exhibit superior performance in mitigating soil thermal imbalance due to the additional solar heat input, but this advantage is accompanied by longer payback periods and higher lifecycle costs. In contrast, GSHP systems can alleviate thermal interference through borehole spacing optimization, thereby improving thermal performance without introducing additional system complexity or significant investment increases. This indicates that, although SGSHP systems rely on external energy input to enhance thermal performance, optimized GSHP systems can achieve a comparable level of soil thermal regulation through structural design adjustments alone. As a result, GSHP systems with appropriate borehole spacing provide a more economically attractive solution under the studied conditions.

In this work, the underground pipe spacings of a GSHP system and an SGSHP system were investigated to compare the effects of different underground pipe spacings on the heat accumulation characteristics of the pipes in the fork mode. The soil surface temperature characteristics were also analyzed.
(1)
The simulation results for the heat transfer performance show that the heat balance in both GSHP and SGSHP systems decreases with increases in the underground pipe spacing, and the heat transfer processes of both systems improved. This indicates that underground pipe spacing optimization benefits both systems. The advantage of the SGSHP system is that it reduces the geothermal imbalance. The thermal imbalance gap between the two systems can be narrowed by simply increasing the underground pipe spacing.
(2)
The results of the economic analysis show that an increase in the underground pipe spacing that remains within 5 m does not lead to a significant reduction in the economic viability. When the underground pipe spacing is more than 5 m, the economic viability of the GSHP system will be reduced significantly and the investment period for dynamic recovery will be extended considerably, to more than 35 years. Thus, the economic viability is greatly reduced.

The conclusion drawn from the analysis above is that increasing the underground pipe spacing helps to narrow the thermal balance gap between the GSHP and SGSHP systems, thus improving the overall system thermal performance. From an economic perspective, increasing the spacing to 5 m does not affect the GSHP system’s cost-effectiveness significantly. Therefore, optimizing the underground pipe spacing can effectively balance the enhanced heat transfer efficiency with the economic viability of the system.

This study provides actionable insights into the deployment of GSHP and SGSHP systems in cold regions with limited solar availability, such as northern China. From a system-level perspective, SGSHP systems are effective in mitigating long-term soil thermal imbalance and enhancing seasonal heat storage through solar energy injection. From a broader perspective, the performance improvement brought by solar integration is not absolute but strongly dependent on boundary conditions. The effectiveness of solar thermal collectors is influenced by local solar radiation levels, heating demand duration, and energy prices, which jointly determine whether the additional solar input can offset the increased system cost. Therefore, the role of solar-assisted systems should be interpreted in a context-dependent manner rather than as a universally superior solution.

In cold regions with relatively low solar radiation and long heating seasons, the SGSHP system exhibits higher capital investment and increased lifecycle costs, mainly due to solar collector installation, replacement, and additional land use requirements. Therefore, while SGSHP improves thermal sustainability under these specific conditions, its overall economic performance is inferior to that of an optimized GSHP system in the present case.

Another key finding of this work is that optimizing borehole spacing provides a more cost-effective strategy for improving system performance. Increasing the spacing reduces thermal interference between boreholes and effectively alleviates soil heat accumulation. In particular, a spacing of 4.6 m achieves a favorable balance between thermal performance improvement and additional construction cost.

Overall, although solar-assisted GSHP systems offer enhanced environmental benefits at the system level, their economic advantage is not universally guaranteed and is highly dependent on local climatic conditions and solar resource availability. In contrast, conventional GSHP systems with optimized design parameters can achieve comparable thermal performance with superior economic feasibility in cold-region applications. These findings provide practical guidance for engineers and policymakers in selecting appropriate ground source heat pump configurations for similar climatic regions.
